_comment: The Fix-issues prompt model: depth levels + the scope/action text blocks the wizard assembles into the agent prompt. Single source for both front-ends; the assembly order/conditions live as a tiny glue layer in each (see Issues.swift / issues.py). Every prompt here works ONE issue, because a Fix-issues sweep is expanded by the front-end into one queued run per issue rather than one agent told to work a whole scope — the scope selector decides which issues get queued, and never reaches the prompt. Two of the blocks are what a swept issue carries that a hand-named one does not (its state re-checked, and its assignee re-checked), because hours can pass between the sweep picking it up and its turn coming; the rest are the toggles deciding what the run may DO about what it finds.

depths.title: Quick pass
depths.blurb: Fix it only where the code makes the cause unambiguous. Nothing is run.
depths.fragment: Do a QUICK PASS on this issue: read the report, find the code it actually names, and fix it only if its cause is unambiguous from reading that code — a wrong constant, an inverted condition, a missing guard whose absence is visible on the page. You don't need to run or reproduce anything at this depth. The flip side is that you must be honest about the limit: a cause you cannot pin down by reading is one you LEAVE ALONE and report as needing a deeper pass, never one you guess at.

depths.title: Reproduce & fix
depths.blurb: A concrete repro before the fix, and the same one again after it.
depths.fragment: Build a CONCRETE REPRODUCTION from the report before you change anything — precise inputs / steps → the wrong behaviour, run for real — so you have proof the bug exists and proof of what it does. Then develop the fix, and re-run that SAME reproduction to confirm it lands. An issue you cannot reproduce is not fixed: say so, rather than shipping a change against a guess.

depths.title: Deep · swarm the fix
depths.blurb: Repro before & after; swarm the review moves over your own fix.
depths.fragment: Build a CONCRETE REPRODUCTION from the report before you touch anything, develop the fix, and re-run that SAME reproduction to confirm it lands. Then put your own fix through the review moves in my CLAUDE.md with a swarm of agents (3–8) — claims vs code, nearest twin, non-happy paths, inputs, reachability both ways, and what outlives the call — plus the absence pass (a sibling that has it, prose that promises it, symmetry, and the mutation). Treat what the swarm returns as leads, not verdicts: confirm each against the code, fix what is real, and keep dispatching fresh swarms until one full pass comes back clean.

depths.title: Full E2E · max
depths.blurb: Drive the bug in the real app; swarm until one clean pass.
depths.fragment: Maximum rigor. "Reproduced" has a strict meaning here: DRIVE THE BUG THROUGH THE REAL ENTRY POINT and watch the failure happen first-hand — run the actual app (booting a simulator / emulator where the bug needs one) and trigger the fault for real. A code-reading argument, a mock, a stub or an isolated unit test does NOT clear this bar. Fix it, then re-run that same end-to-end reproduction to prove the fix lands. Put your own fix through the review moves in my CLAUDE.md with swarms of agents — claims vs code, nearest twin, non-happy paths, inputs, reachability both ways, and what outlives the call — plus the absence pass (a sibling that has it, prose that promises it, symmetry, and the mutation). Keep dispatching swarms until ONE pass comes back clean — that single clean pass ends the loop, so do not run a confirmation pass on top of it.

scope.single: Take issue #{issue} in {owner}/{repo}, and work that ONE issue — nothing else in the repo's issue list is this run's business. Use the `gh` CLI to fetch it (`gh issue view {issue} --repo {owner}/{repo} --comments`), including every comment on it — a follow-up comment routinely carries the reproduction, the version, or the correction the opening post lacks.

blocks.swept: THIS ISSUE CAME OUT OF A SWEEP, and its turn may have come hours after the sweep picked it up. Before you touch anything, read its CURRENT state off the fetch above: if it has been closed since, somebody has already dealt with it — stop there, change nothing, post nothing, and report it as skipped.
blocks.unassigned: IT WAS ALSO UNASSIGNED WHEN THE SWEEP PICKED IT UP, and only unassigned issues are in scope for this run. Check its assignee list again now: if anybody holds it, it is theirs to work — stop there, change nothing, post nothing, and report it as skipped. An issue assigned to me counts as assigned too, because something is already handling it.
blocks.assignSelf: CLAIM THE ISSUE BEFORE YOU START ON IT: assign it to me — `gh issue edit {issue} --repo {owner}/{repo} --add-assignee @me` — and only then begin the work. This is what stops a second agent (or a person) starting the same issue while you are on it, so it happens FIRST, before the reproduction, not once you have a fix. If you end up abandoning it — you could not reproduce it, it turned out to be out of scope, you ran out of road — remove yourself again (`--remove-assignee @me`) so it goes back into the unassigned pool instead of sitting claimed by nobody working it.
blocks.bugsOnly: ONLY A REAL BUG REPORT IS IN SCOPE. Decide what this issue actually is: a bug report describes something that behaves wrongly. A feature request, enhancement proposal, design discussion, question, support request or wishlist item is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE and must not be worked, however easy it looks — stop there and report it as skipped. When it is ambiguous, treat it as out of scope and say so rather than implementing something nobody asked you to.
blocks.includeFeatures: A FEATURE REQUEST IS IN SCOPE TOO on this run, not only a bug report — but it is held to a different standard than a bug, because a bug has a right answer and a feature does not. Take an enhancement on ONLY when the issue states clearly enough what is wanted that you can build the thing the reporter actually asked for, and when it fits how this codebase already works: extend or compose what is there rather than introducing a parallel abstraction beside it. Anything vague, speculative, or amounting to a redesign gets left alone and named in the report as needing a decision from me — that call is mine, not yours. A question, a support request or pure discussion is still out of scope.
blocks.bar: Hold to the bar in my CLAUDE.md throughout. DONE MEANS OBSERVABLE PROOF, never "should work": the fix counts only once the same reproduction that showed the bug is re-run and comes back clean, and you say which verification you ran. Fix the CLASS, not the instance — search the repo for every other call site, sibling backend or adjacent path of the same shape and fix them together, or name each one you are leaving and why. Bring every piece of prose the change touches into agreement with the new behaviour, and write it as a description of the code as it now stands, never as a narration of what changed. Delete anything the fix made unreachable. And run the project's own checks — format, lint, typecheck, tests, build — before you call it done.
blocks.cannotReproduce: AN ISSUE YOU CANNOT REPRODUCE IS NOT A FAILURE OF THE RUN — it is a result, and it has to be reported as one. Never paper over it with a speculative change: no fix goes in on a bug you were unable to make happen. Say exactly what you tried (the steps, the version, the environment) and what you observed instead, so the gap is something I can act on.
blocks.openPRs: Deliver the fix as its own focused pull request, opened as a DRAFT (`gh pr create --draft`) — ALWAYS draft, never a ready-for-review PR, and never mark it ready yourself. It closes the issue it fixes: put a closing reference (`Fixes #{issue}`) in its description, and give it a title and description that name the defect and quote the evidence — the reproduction that proved the bug, and the same reproduction re-run clean after the fix. SHIP A REGRESSION TEST WITH THE FIX, one that pins the exact behaviour it corrected: you established the wrong value when you reproduced the bug and the right one when you confirmed the fix, so assert the right one in a way the wrong one would VIOLATE (an exact value, count, order, type or status code — never an incidental property like `>= 1` or `contains something`, which the unfixed code already satisfied). Do not undo or weaken the fix to check that; argue it from the reproduction you already captured. RIGHT BEFORE you open it, verify it is NOT a DUPLICATE of an existing open PR — this issue may already have one, and other agents are working the repo's other issues alongside you: enumerate the repo's open PRs and compare their ACTUAL CODE, not their titles or descriptions (those routinely mislead), reading each plausible candidate's real diff with `gh pr diff <n>`. If one already lands the same fix, do NOT open a duplicate: skip it and tell me which PR already covers it.
blocks.noPRs: This run opens NO pull requests and pushes NOTHING: do not commit, do not push, do not open a PR. Keep the fix in the working tree and hand it to me in the report — which files it touches, what it changes, and the reproduction you ran before and after it. Nothing reaches the remote.
blocks.comment: Report the outcome ON THE ISSUE ITSELF (`gh issue comment {issue} --repo {owner}/{repo}`), so the reporter learns what happened without waiting for me. Say what you reproduced, what the cause turned out to be, and where the fix is — the PR number when there is one. If you could not reproduce it, say what you tried and what you saw instead, and ask for the one specific detail that would let you get further. Never post a bare "fixed" or "cannot reproduce" with nothing behind it, and post nothing at all on an issue you stopped short of working.
blocks.noAttribution: No AI attribution anywhere in git/GitHub — commits and PRs authored as me, no Co-Authored-By, no "Generated with" taglines.
blocks.diplomatTag: Diplomat attribution tag — a REQUIRED exception to the no-attribution rule, for GitHub commentary only. Do NOT tag PR titles — leave every pull-request title exactly as you would write it. End every pull-request DESCRIPTION with a footer: after the body, a blank line, a horizontal rule on its own line (`---`), a blank line, then this exact last line — `<sub>Made by Diplomat. Like what you're seeing? [Give it a try](https://github.com/latekvo/Diplomat).</sub>`. In that footer the word Diplomat is PLAIN TEXT (not a link); ONLY "Give it a try" is a Markdown link, pointing to https://github.com/latekvo/Diplomat. For every standalone comment you post instead (an issue comment, or a review / reply comment), BEGIN it with the exact prefix `\[[Diplomat](https://github.com/latekvo/Diplomat){model}\]: `, copied character for character — the `\[` and `\]` are literal brackets, only the word Diplomat is a Markdown link (to https://github.com/latekvo/Diplomat), anything after that link is plain text, and a colon and a space close it — followed by the text you would otherwise have written, so it renders as "[Diplomat{model}]: <your text>". This is the ONE sanctioned attribution; it applies to posted PR-description / comment text ONLY and never changes PR titles, commit messages, commit authorship, or the no-Co-Authored-By / no-"Generated with" git rules, which remain in force.
blocks.summary: At the very end, give me one report on issue #{issue} — it is the whole of this run's work, so put it in exactly one bucket: fixed (with the reproduction you ran and where the fix landed), reproduced but not fixed (and what stopped you), could not reproduce (what you tried, what you saw), or skipped (which rule above took it out — closed since, claimed by somebody else, not a bug).
